A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same judge-tuning study despite the changed title. All 14 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original scaling experiments, analysis of 4,480 judge configurations, and preliminary LMSys and PandaLM test results.

after.justification: v3 reports original scaling and tuning experiments, updated test results, an additional Arena-Hard comparison, and fidelity-stability analysis.

M1.justification: Both retain the 4,480-configuration search, prompt options, three-stage successive halving and non-dominated sorting for accuracy and cost. Synchronous execution and epsilon-net tie-breaking are newly documented in v3, without evidence that they replace an earlier procedure.

E1.justification: Both use Alpaca-Eval, Arena-Hard, Chatbot Arena ratings, LMSys and PandaLM for preference judging and model ranking. v3 evaluates tuned judges on the already-covered Arena-Hard ranking task; changes in model subsets and annotation counts concern evaluation settings.

E2.justification: v3 adds a direct comparison against Arena-Hard judges using Claude Opus and GPT-4-1106-preview in Table 4, substantially expanding comparison with frontier judges. The LMSys comparator set is retained: its shortened Arena-Hard label still denotes GPT-4o mini. A Random comparator is also added to the PandaLM table.

E3.justification: Test-judge selection advances from v1's explicitly preliminary 1,200-instruction stage to the full 3,548-instruction validation set. Table 1 replaces 400 instructions times 24 models versus 6,400 human-agreement battles with 6,500 annotations for each metric, using 26 models for Spearman correlation. v3 also introduces the tuned-judge comparison on 20 models and 500 Arena-Hard instructions. Appendix B.1 replaces TogetherAI token prices with runtime-derived self-hosting estimates, materially changing the cost evaluation.

E4.justification: New Figure 13 tests split-half stability of judge scores at the three fidelity sizes, providing focused evidence about ranking reliability. Figure 7 updates the existing prompt-stability analysis, and the Impact Statement reports a limited qualitative inspection of LMSys data. The main hyperparameter-survival analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports variability for scaling metrics but only point estimates in its test-comparison tables. v3 adds 100-bootstrap uncertainty reporting for LMSys and the Arena-Hard comparison, plus coefficients of variation in Table 1. These are resampling procedures, not evidence of 100 independent tuning runs. LMSys prose calls the uncertainty standard errors while its caption calls it standard deviation.

E6.justification: Test results are substantially expanded and revised. LMSys JudgeLM-7B changes from 0.440 to 0.42, and a large tuned judge is added at 0.49. The largest tuned judge's PandaLM score changes from 0.74 to 0.76. New Table 4 reports Arena-Hard correlations of 0.81, 0.93 and 0.86 for the three tuned judges, versus 0.82 for Claude and 0.90 for GPT-4. Scaling and prompt-correlation values also change. Revised selection, sampling and cost assumptions prevent treating these collectively as same-setting gains.

T1.justification: New Appendix C formally defines multi-objective optimization, dominance and the Pareto front, and discusses scalarization restrictions and non-dominated sorting. This adds mathematical background and reasoning, but no new theorem or proof about the proposed tuning method.

C1.justification: The main contributions remain scaling analysis, affordable multi-objective multi-fidelity tuning, competitive open-weight judges, and analysis of judge design choices. The new title foregrounds an approximately 1,000-fold cost reduction, but v1 Appendix B.3 already supplied the roughly $2.1K versus $2M estimates supporting that claim.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly qualifies that fine-tuning might improve PandaLM performance while hurting generalization. Its new Impact Statement discusses propagation of human and group biases and limits the reassurance obtainable from its small LMSys inspection. Existing explanations involving model capacity, prompt complexity and distribution shift are largely retained.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents synchronous scheduling across two cluster queues, epsilon-net tie-breaking, and per-model runtime-derived token prices in Table 6. It also revises hardware-price and annotation-time assumptions. Prompt examples and split instructions remain, and both versions still promise future code and annotation release.

R1.justification: v3 adds Zhang et al. on summarization, Ni et al. on LEVER, and Elshin et al. on translation, while removing the Verga et al. jury reference. The positioning relative to zero-shot judges, fine-tuned judges and prompt optimization remains substantially unchanged. The Llama 3 author correction identifies the same cited work.

P1.justification: Paragraphs across the introduction, related work, metric explanations, test-results discussion and conclusion are extensively edited or rewritten. v3 changes the title, replaces the preliminary-results narrative, and adds Impact Statement, Acknowledgments and multi-objective-background sections, while retaining the main numbered section sequence.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the displays: the search-space table moves to the appendix, Figure 6 combines separate model-size panels into grouped bars, and Table 1 replaces cost entries with variability columns. Test tables gain uncertainty and revised cost units. New displays include the Arena-Hard comparison, token-price table, sorting illustration, recolored configuration plots and fidelity-stability plots.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly bases its preliminary test results on an unfinished search. v3 reports selection using the full validation set, directly evaluates the tuned judges' Arena-Hard rankings, and adds bootstrap uncertainty and fidelity-stability evidence. These substantially strengthen validation of the proposed approach. Changed cost assumptions limit interpretation of the lower dollar figures, and the PandaLM prose still claims outperformance where the small judge and PandaLM-70B both score 0.67, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.
